Decatur.wildlife_intro:
Decatur is the historic seat of DeKalb County and one of metro Atlanta's most established intown small cities, with a wildlife-pressure profile driven almost entirely by its dense canopy of mature hardwoods and its early-1900s housing stock. The Oakhurst, Winnona Park, and MAK historic districts are wall-to-wall Craftsman bungalows and Tudor cottages from the 1910s through the 1930s — a construction era that produces a textbook multi-entry-point profile: original unscreened gable vents, deep wood soffits and fascia that rot and gap, knee-wall attic voids behind upstairs rooms, low brick-pier crawl spaces, and original masonry chimneys without modern caps. Eastern gray squirrels dominate Decatur call volume because the oak-and-hickory canopy over Oakhurst and Winnona Park is among the densest in the county, feeding a large resident population that moves into attics through soffit and gable gaps each fall and again in late winter. Raccoons are the second-heaviest call, concentrating in homes with uncapped chimneys and along the wooded edges near Legacy Park and the Agnes Scott campus, with denning pressure peaking during whelping from late February through May.

The Agnes Scott College campus and the nearby Emory University corridor add a year-round, dumpster-driven layer to the call mix — student-housing and food-service waste sustains urban raccoons, Norway rats, and Virginia opossums that radiate into the surrounding bungalow blocks. Older Decatur homes with original masonry chimneys not uncommonly host bat roosts (big brown and evening bats are the species most often found in intown DeKalb structures), and roof rats are well established in the older intown housing, traveling power lines and overhanging limbs into attics. Southern flying squirrels turn up at lower volume but are routine in Decatur's canopy, giving themselves away by faint night-time scratching in walls. Along the creek corridors and wooded park edges, homeowners also report snakes (almost all non-venomous rat snakes and garter snakes) and occasional coyote sightings moving through at night.

Decatur Animal Control vs. Private Wildlife Removal — Who to Call

Decatur homeowners often call DeKalb County Animal Services first, then learn that county animal control here handles domestic-animal matters — stray dogs and cats, bite reports, leash-law complaints — and generally does not respond to nuisance wildlife living in attics, chimneys, walls, or crawl spaces. Matching the situation to the right contact saves a call:

  • Domestic-animal issues (stray dog, cat bite, leash complaint) — DeKalb County Animal Services. Free.
  • Injured or orphaned wildlife (a fallen baby bird, a fawn, a sick raccoon) — a permitted Georgia DNR wildlife rehabilitator. Free or donation-based.
  • Rabies-vector exposure (a bat found in a bedroom, a bite or scratch from any mammal) — the DeKalb County Board of Health and your physician or veterinarian. Insurance-billed.
  • Nuisance wildlife removal and exclusion (squirrels in the bungalow attic, raccoons in the chimney, bats, rats chewing wiring, snakes in the crawl space) — a licensed private contractor. Paid service.

faqs.q: What wildlife is most common in Decatur homes?
faqs.a: Eastern gray squirrels lead Decatur call volume by a wide margin — the dense oak-and-hickory canopy over Oakhurst and Winnona Park feeds a large population that pushes into bungalow attics through soffit and gable gaps each fall and late winter. Raccoons are second, concentrating in homes with uncapped chimneys and along the wooded edges near Legacy Park and Agnes Scott, peaking during whelping from late February through May. Roof and Norway rats are well established in the older intown housing, bats roost in some original masonry chimneys, and southern flying squirrels and the occasional snake round out the routine mix.

faqs.q: Why do Decatur's old bungalows have so many wildlife problems?
faqs.a: It comes down to the 1910s-1930s construction era. Craftsman and Tudor homes in Oakhurst, Winnona Park, and MAK were built with deep wood soffits and fascia that rot and separate over a century, original unscreened gable vents, knee-wall attic voids tucked behind upstairs rooms, low brick-pier crawl spaces, and uncapped masonry chimneys. Each of those is a ready-made entry point. Squirrels and rats exploit the soffit and gable gaps; raccoons drop down the open chimneys; flying squirrels slip through the smallest openings. Permanent results in Decatur almost always mean sealing the whole roofline, not just trapping the animal inside.

faqs.q: How can I tell whether it's squirrels or rats in my attic?
faqs.a: Timing is the fastest tell. Squirrels are daytime animals — quick, busy scampering you hear most at dawn and again in late afternoon, with the heaviest activity in fall and late winter. Rats are nocturnal — lighter, faster movement plus gnawing and scratching that you notice after dark and in the walls as much as the attic. Squirrel droppings are larger and rounder; rat droppings are smaller and spindle-shaped. Flying squirrels, common in Decatur's canopy, are also nocturnal but gliding and gentler-sounding. A licensed inspection confirms the species by entry points and dropping morphology before any exclusion work begins.

faqs.q: There's a bat flying in my house — what should I do?
faqs.a: Don't swat at it. Confine it to one room by closing interior doors, then open an exterior window or door in that room, dim the lights, and give it a clear path out. The critical question is whether anyone — especially a child, a deep sleeper, or someone unable to reliably say they weren't touched — may have had unnoticed contact, because a bat in a bedroom is treated as presumptive rabies exposure even without an obvious bite. In that case the bat should be safely captured without crushing its head so the DeKalb County Board of Health can arrange testing, and you should call your physician. Then bring in a licensed contractor to find the roost and the entry point.

faqs.q: Is it safe to seal up the entry point myself?
faqs.a: Sealing minor gaps outside of breeding season is reasonable homeowner scope; sealing during active maternity season is the most common DIY backfire in Decatur. Seal a squirrel or raccoon entry from roughly late February through May, or a bat entry from mid-May through July or August, and you trap dependent young inside the cavity — the result is a decomposition and odor problem that costs far more to remediate than the original exclusion would have. Bat exclusion is also timing-regulated by Georgia DNR and should only proceed in the approved window. When in doubt on a 1920s bungalow, a licensed inspection will tell you whether young are present before anything gets closed.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Decatur?
faqs.a: Cost depends on the species, the size and age of the home, the number of entry points, and whether decontamination is needed — Decatur's century-old bungalows often have more entry points than newer construction. Rather than quote a generic range, we give you a firm price after a free phone consultation and on-site inspection. Both are no-charge, so you'll know the scope and the number before any work is scheduled.

faqs.q: Will my homeowners insurance cover the damage?
faqs.a: Most Georgia policies exclude the removal of the animal itself as a pest or maintenance item, but they frequently cover sudden resulting damage when the relevant peril is included — chewed wiring, soiled or torn insulation, damaged soffits and shingles, and contamination cleanup are often covered when documented as caused by the wildlife event. Keep dated photos of every entry point and damaged area and hold onto the contractor's written inspection report, since carriers usually want the report's species identification and damage scope. Coverage varies by carrier and policy, so call your agent with the report in hand before assuming either way.

faqs.q: How quickly can someone come out in Decatur?
faqs.a: Same-day inspection is standard for Decatur calls. True emergencies — a bat loose in living space, a raccoon visibly inside the home, an injured animal — get 24/7 response and jump ahead of the routine queue. Standard exclusion work, like full-roofline squirrel sealing on an Oakhurst bungalow or a chimney raccoon job, typically schedules within a few business days. Whelping- and maternity-season calls from late February through May are expedited because the legal timing constraints on what can proceed make every day count.

Dunwoody.wildlife_intro:
Dunwoody occupies the wooded northern tip of DeKalb County, where one of metro Atlanta's busiest commercial cores — the Perimeter Center district along I-285 and GA-400 — sits directly against heavily forested mid-century residential streets. That juxtaposition defines the city's wildlife profile. The 1960s-1980s ranch and split-level subdivisions of Dunwoody Club Forest, Branches, Kingsley, and Vanderlyn were built on large wooded lots under a dense hardwood canopy, and many back onto creek buffers and protected woods. The result is heavy, year-round pressure from canopy and forest-edge species. Eastern gray squirrels top Dunwoody call volume, exploiting the wood and aluminum soffits, ridge vents, and gable vents typical of mid-century construction. Raccoons are the second-largest category and a particular problem here because the wooded buffers and the food sources around Perimeter Center sustain a large, well-fed population; they den in chimneys, attics, and under decks, with whelping pressure heaviest from late February through May.

The Nancy Creek corridor and the preserved forest at Brook Run Park and the Dunwoody Nature Center act as continuous source habitat, feeding wildlife into adjoining neighborhoods. Along these creek and woodland corridors, Dunwoody homeowners report beavers damming culverts and small streams, coyotes moving through at night, and the full intown roster of Virginia opossums and snakes (predominantly non-venomous rat snakes and garter snakes). Bats — big brown and evening bats — roost in some homes, drawn to ridge gaps and gable louvers, and the city's many large attics make ideal maternity roosts. Roof rats are established in the wooded residential areas, using overhanging limbs and utility lines as highways into attics, while southern flying squirrels are common in the canopy and account for a meaningful share of the nighttime-scratching calls that homeowners first assume are rats. New-construction homes from the 1990s onward see fewer entry points but are not immune, especially where attached garages and gable returns meet the roofline.

Dunwoody Animal Control vs. Private Wildlife Removal — What to Expect

Dunwoody residents frequently call DeKalb County Animal Services first, only to learn that county animal control handles domestic-animal complaints — strays, bites, and leash issues — and does not typically remove nuisance wildlife from attics, chimneys, decks, or yards. Here's who actually handles each situation:

  • Domestic-animal issues (stray dog, cat bite, leash complaint) — DeKalb County Animal Services. Free.
  • Injured or orphaned wildlife (an orphaned fawn near Brook Run, a fallen baby bird, a sick raccoon) — a permitted Georgia DNR wildlife rehabilitator. Free or donation-based.
  • Rabies-vector exposure (a bat in the bedroom, a bite or scratch from any mammal) — the DeKalb County Board of Health and your physician or veterinarian. Insurance-billed.
  • Nuisance wildlife removal and exclusion (raccoons in the chimney, squirrels in the attic, beavers in a creek culvert, bats, rats, snakes) — a licensed private contractor. Paid service.

faqs.q: What wildlife is most common in Dunwoody?
faqs.a: Eastern gray squirrels lead Dunwoody calls because nearly every neighborhood sits under a dense hardwood canopy that feeds a large resident population straight into mid-century soffits and ridge vents. Raccoons are a close second and a heavier problem here than in many DeKalb cities, sustained by the wooded creek buffers and the food sources around Perimeter Center. Along Nancy Creek and the Brook Run and Nature Center woods, homeowners also see beavers, coyotes, and opossums. Bats roost in some homes, roof rats use overhanging limbs as highways into attics, and southern flying squirrels are routine in the canopy.

faqs.q: Why are raccoons such a big problem in Dunwoody?
faqs.a: Dunwoody combines two things raccoons thrive on: extensive wooded creek buffers for denning and a dense, food-rich commercial district at Perimeter Center. That supports a large, well-fed population that pushes into neighborhoods to den in chimneys, attics, and under decks. The heaviest window is whelping, late February through May, when females seek quiet, enclosed cavities to raise kits — an uncapped chimney or an open soffit is ideal. Because kits stay dependent for weeks, an active den can't legally be sealed during that period without trapping the young inside, which is why timing matters and why a licensed inspection comes first.

faqs.q: I hear scratching at night — is it rats or flying squirrels?
faqs.a: In Dunwoody it's often flying squirrels, which are easy to mistake for rats. Both are nocturnal, but flying squirrels are gliding canopy animals that tend to be active in short bursts right after dark and again before dawn, often with a faint thumping as they land in the attic. Rats move more continuously through the night and gnaw persistently, frequently inside wall voids rather than the open attic. Dunwoody's deep tree canopy makes flying squirrels genuinely common. The reliable way to know is a licensed inspection — entry-point size, droppings, and runways distinguish the two before exclusion begins.

faqs.q: There's a beaver damming a creek near my Dunwoody home — who handles that?
faqs.a: Beaver activity along Nancy Creek and the smaller streams in Dunwoody is a recurring issue, and it's not something county animal control addresses. Beaver dams can flood culverts, back water onto yards, and topple streamside trees. A licensed nuisance-wildlife contractor handles assessment, dam management, and trapping where appropriate, working within Georgia DNR regulations. Because beaver work often involves flowing water, drainage easements, and sometimes shared or HOA-owned land, it's worth a professional assessment before anyone modifies a dam — improperly pulling a dam can make flooding worse and may run afoul of stream-buffer rules.

faqs.q: Do new-construction Dunwoody homes get wildlife too?
faqs.a: Yes, though less often than the 1960s-1980s housing. Newer two-story and infill homes have tighter envelopes, but they still sit under the same canopy and back onto the same wooded buffers, so the pressure is identical. The weak points shift: instead of failing wood soffits, problems tend to appear where attached garages meet the house, at gable returns, around poorly screened ridge vents, and at construction gaps that were never fully closed. Squirrels and roof rats find these readily. A roofline inspection catches them, and sealing is usually quicker on newer homes because there are fewer total openings.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Dunwoody?
faqs.a: Pricing depends on the species, the home, the number of entry points, and whether decontamination is required — a single squirrel entry on a newer home is very different from a multi-entry raccoon or bat job on a wooded mid-century house. We don't quote blind. After a free phone consultation and a free on-site inspection, you get a firm price for the specific scope, so there are no surprises before any work is scheduled.

faqs.q: How fast can a contractor reach my Dunwoody home?
faqs.a: Same-day inspection is standard across Dunwoody. Emergencies — a bat flying in living space, a raccoon inside the home, an injured animal in the yard — get 24/7 priority response ahead of the routine queue. Standard exclusion jobs, like sealing a full roofline against squirrels or evicting raccoons from a chimney, generally schedule within a few business days. Spring whelping and summer bat-maternity calls are expedited because the legal timing windows under Georgia DNR rules limit when exclusion can safely and lawfully proceed.

  • Injured or orphaned wildlife (a fallen nestling, an orphaned fawn near Murphey Candler, a sick raccoon) — a permitted Georgia DNR wildlife rehabilitator. Free or donation-based.

The newer luxury and townhome construction near Dresden and Town Brookhaven has tighter envelopes, so total entry points are fewer — but the same canopy and creek buffers sit right outside, so squirrels and roof rats still exploit construction gaps at garages, gable returns, and ridge vents. The species mix is similar citywide; what changes is where the entry points are and how many there are.

faqs.q: How do I know if a raccoon is denning in my chimney?
faqs.a: The clearest signs are sound and smell. A denning raccoon produces a slow, heavy footfall and shuffling in the chimney chase at dusk and again before dawn, and during whelping season you may hear the high, bird-like chittering of kits. A musky ammonia odor pushing down through the firebox or into a nearby room is a strong second indicator. From outside, look for a missing or dislodged chimney cap and claw marks on the masonry. Brookhaven's older estate homes are classic candidates. A licensed contractor confirms it, evicts humanely, and caps the chimney so it can't recur.

faqs.q: I think there's a beaver near Murphey Candler Park flooding my property — what now?

A contractor handles assessment, lawful trapping, and ongoing dam management as needed.

faqs.q: Are bats in my attic dangerous?
faqs.a: The risk while a bat colony stays in the attic is mainly environmental rather than an immediate threat to people. Accumulated guano can support Histoplasma capsulatum, the fungus behind histoplasmosis, especially in long-established roosts in older Brookhaven homes. The acute concern is a single bat that enters living space — a bat in a bedroom is treated as presumptive rabies exposure for anyone who can't reliably rule out contact, including sleepers and children, because bat bites can be tiny. In that situation, capture the bat without crushing its head for Board of Health testing and call your physician. Colony removal then requires timed, Georgia DNR-compliant exclusion plus HEPA-grade cleanup.

The safe approach to any snake you can't confidently identify is to keep your distance and call a licensed contractor for identification and removal rather than attempting to handle or kill it, since most bites happen during those attempts.

faqs.q: I hear something in my attic during the day — what is it?
faqs.a: Daytime activity in a Tucker attic points strongly to squirrels. Eastern gray squirrels are diurnal, most active at dawn and in the late afternoon, and produce quick, busy scampering and rolling sounds — sometimes the noise of stored acorns. The heaviest indoor activity comes in fall and again in late winter. Nocturnal scratching, by contrast, usually means rats or southern flying squirrels, both of which are common in Tucker's canopy. A licensed inspection confirms the species by entry-point size, droppings, and runways, which matters because squirrel and rat exclusion are handled differently.

faqs.q: How do raccoons get into Tucker post-war homes?
faqs.a: The 1950s-1970s ranches and split-levels that make up most of Tucker offer raccoons several routes: uncapped masonry chimneys they climb down, gaps where aluminum soffits have separated, weak gable returns, and the sheltered spaces under carports and low decks. Whelping season, late February through May, is when females actively seek these enclosed cavities to raise kits, so it's the heaviest denning window. Because kits remain dependent for weeks, an active den can't be sealed during that period without trapping the young inside. A licensed contractor inspects, evicts humanely, and caps or seals the access points to prevent return.

faqs.q: Can a beaver really be a problem in suburban Tucker?
faqs.a: Yes — the smaller streams and creek corridors threading through Tucker's wooded areas support beavers, and their dams can flood culverts, back water onto yards, and topple streamside trees. This isn't a county animal-control matter; it's handled by a licensed nuisance-wildlife contractor working within Georgia DNR rules. Because the work involves flowing water, drainage easements, and sometimes shared or HOA land, it should begin with a professional assessment — pulling a dam improperly can make flooding worse and may run afoul of stream-buffer regulations. A contractor handles assessment, lawful trapping, and dam management as needed.

Chamblee.wildlife_intro:
Chamblee occupies the northern edge of DeKalb County, where a historic rail-town core — anchored by the antique district known as Antique Row and the surrounding early-1900s bungalows — meets the dense, fast-changing Buford Highway corridor and a wave of new infill construction. That mix of old and new, residential and commercial, defines the city's wildlife profile. The 1910s-1940s bungalows and cottages near downtown, with their wood soffits, unscreened vents, and original masonry chimneys, are prime entry-point candidates, and the mature canopy around Keswick Park, Sexton Woods, and Huntley Hills makes Eastern gray squirrels the leading Chamblee call. Squirrels move into the older attics through soffit and gable gaps each fall and late winter. Raccoons are the second-heaviest category, denning in the bungalows' uncapped chimneys and along the wooded creek edges, with whelping concentrated from late February through May.

The Buford Highway corridor's dense commercial and multi-family development is a distinctive driver here: its restaurants, markets, and dumpsters sustain a large, well-fed population of urban raccoons, Norway rats, and Virginia opossums that radiate into the surrounding residential blocks — a heavier urban-rodent pressure than the more strictly residential DeKalb cities see. The Nancy Creek corridor threading through Chamblee adds forest-edge habitat, and along it homeowners report beavers on the smaller channels, occasional coyotes at night, and non-venomous snakes (rat snakes and garter snakes). Roof rats are firmly established across the older bungalow housing and the corridor, using utility lines and overhanging limbs into attics, and bats — big brown and evening bats — roost in some of the older homes through gable louvers and ridge gaps. Southern flying squirrels are routine in the canopy and behind many of the nighttime-scratching calls homeowners first attribute to rats. The new townhomes and modern infill near downtown and the MARTA station have tighter envelopes, but they sit in the same setting, so squirrels and rats still exploit construction gaps at garages and gable returns.

Chamblee Animal Control vs. Private Wildlife Removal — What to Know

Chamblee homeowners commonly call DeKalb County Animal Services first, then learn that county animal control handles domestic-animal complaints — strays, bites, leash issues — and does not remove nuisance wildlife from attics, chimneys, walls, or yards. Here's who actually handles each situation:

  • Domestic-animal issues (stray dog, cat bite, leash complaint) — DeKalb County Animal Services. Free.
  • Injured or orphaned wildlife (a fallen baby bird, an orphaned fawn, a sick raccoon) — a permitted Georgia DNR wildlife rehabilitator. Free or donation-based.
  • Rabies-vector exposure (a bat found in a bedroom, a bite or scratch from any mammal) — the DeKalb County Board of Health and your physician or veterinarian. Insurance-billed.
  • Nuisance wildlife removal and exclusion (squirrels and rats in the attic, raccoons in the chimney, bats, snakes, beavers on Nancy Creek) — a licensed private contractor. Paid service.

faqs.a: Eastern gray squirrels lead Chamblee calls because the canopy around Keswick Park, Sexton Woods, and Huntley Hills feeds a large population into older bungalow attics. Raccoons are second, denning in uncapped chimneys and along the wooded creek edges. Chamblee stands out for heavy urban-rodent pressure from the Buford Highway corridor, where restaurants and multi-family development sustain Norway rats, raccoons, and opossums. Roof rats are firmly established across the older housing, bats roost in some bungalows, southern flying squirrels are routine in the canopy, and beavers and snakes turn up along the Nancy Creek corridor.

faqs.q: Why does Chamblee have more rats than some nearby cities?
faqs.a: The Buford Highway corridor is the main reason. Its dense concentration of restaurants, markets, and multi-family housing creates a steady, year-round food supply that supports large populations of Norway rats and roof rats, which then radiate into the surrounding residential blocks. Add the older bungalow housing near Antique Row — with its many soffit gaps, crawl spaces, and unscreened vents — and you get conditions rats exploit easily. Effective control in Chamblee almost always pairs exclusion (sealing every entry point) with sanitation guidance, because trapping alone won't keep new rats from following the same food and the same gaps.

faqs.q: How can I tell if it's roof rats or squirrels in my attic?
faqs.a: Timing is the quickest distinction. Squirrels are daytime animals — busy scampering you hear most at dawn and in late afternoon, heaviest in fall and late winter. Roof rats are nocturnal — lighter, faster movement plus persistent gnawing you notice after dark, frequently inside wall voids as much as the attic. Roof rats are excellent climbers and use utility lines and limbs to reach the roof, so entry points are often higher and smaller than a squirrel's. Droppings differ too: squirrel pellets are larger and rounder, rat droppings smaller and spindle-shaped. A licensed inspection confirms which before exclusion.

faqs.q: There's a bat in my Chamblee house — what should I do?
faqs.a: Don't try to swat it. Close interior doors to confine it to one room, open an exterior window or door there, dim the lights, and let it find its way out. The key question is whether anyone — a sleeper, a child, or anyone who can't be certain they weren't touched — may have had unnoticed contact, because a bat in a bedroom counts as presumptive rabies exposure even with no visible bite. If so, capture the bat without crushing its head for DeKalb Board of Health testing and call your physician. Then have a licensed contractor locate the roost and entry point; older Chamblee bungalows can host established colonies.

faqs.q: Do the new Chamblee townhomes get wildlife too?
faqs.a: They can. The modern infill and townhomes near downtown and the MARTA station have tighter building envelopes than the old bungalows, so they have fewer total entry points — but they sit in the same canopy and near the same corridor food sources, so squirrels and rats still test them. The weak spots shift to construction gaps at attached garages, gable returns, poorly screened ridge vents, and utility penetrations. The advantage is that exclusion on newer homes is usually faster, since there are fewer openings to seal once a roofline inspection pinpoints them.

We don't quote blind. After a free phone consultation and a free on-site inspection, you receive a firm price for the exact scope, with no charge to learn what the job involves before scheduling.

Stone Mountain.wildlife_intro:

Stone Mountain Park — thousands of acres of granite outcrop, hardwood and pine forest, and several lakes — wraps the city, so park-adjacent neighborhoods are pressed directly against an enormous, continuous source population. That proximity, combined with a housing mix that runs from 19th-century Victorian and early-1900s homes near Main Street to mid-century ranches and later subdivisions toward the park boundary, gives Stone Mountain a heavy and varied wildlife profile. Eastern gray squirrels lead the call volume, drawn from the park's vast canopy into the older village homes' wood soffits and deep eaves and the post-war homes' gable vents, especially each fall and late winter. Raccoons are a very heavy second category here because the park's forest and lakes sustain a large denning population that moves into uncapped masonry chimneys, attics, and the spaces under decks and carports, with whelping concentrated from late February through May.

Along the lakeshores and the streams feeding them, homeowners report beavers damming channels and culverts, and coyotes are a regular nighttime presence moving between the park and the neighborhoods.
